# HVAC multivariable system modelling and control
Proc IMechE Part C: J Mechanical Engineering Science 2023, Vol. 237(9) 2049–2061 - IMechE 2022 Article reuse guidelines: [sagepub.com/journals-permissions](https://uk.sagepub.com/en-gb/journals-permissions) [DOI: 10.1177/09544062221138836](https://doi.org/10.1177/09544062221138836) [journals.sagepub.com/home/pic](journals.sagepub.com/home/pic)
#### Basim Touqan1 , Alaa Abdul-Ameer1 and Muna Salameh2
### Abstract
Heating, Ventilation and Air Conditioning (HVAC) is a multivariable process where any alteration with one system input affects most or all of the system's outputs simultaneously. Owing to its comprehensiveness, a readily derived multivariable HVAC mathematical model is selected for this work, mainly a hybrid distributed-lumped parameters model. As the transfer function matrix was not established in the selected HVAC model, it was exclusively developed in this study, using the time domain graphical responses of the chosen model. Based on the developed transfer function matrix, a conceptual two-step approach was followed to control HVAC model performance. The first was decoupling the interactions that affect all the system outputs, and the second was designing proper PID controllers for each decoupled loop similar to those used for single input single output (SISO) systems. A direct Nyquist Array (DNA) multivariable control strategy was used for this purpose and successfully decoupled the HVAC system into three separate (SISO) loops. Three PID controllers afterwards were applied for each decoupled loop. The results showed quite decoupled system outputs with a minor coupling percentage so that any change in a system input only affected the corresponding system output. The output responses are also underdamped with almost zero steady-state error confirming the effectiveness of the selected PID parameters. The values of steady-state responses are obtained in (10– 15) s compared with (200–600) s of open-loop response time. However, various overshoot percentages in the responses are encountered but are relatively small, with a short settling time, so they don't affect the thermal comfort of the ventilated volume. System stability using the Nyquist criterion has also been examined and found to satisfy the criterion. The multivariable DNA control technique and the SISO closed-loop PID controllers have shown the capability to suppress external disturbances and restore the system to its original functional steady-state values.
# Keywords
HVAC, transfer function matrix, multivariable control, Direct Nyquist Array, loops decoupling
Date received: 24 June 2022; accepted: 9 October 2022
# Introduction
There are many reasons why (HVAC) systems are considered so important. They are one of the major energy consumers in buildings and account for about 50% of total building energy consumption.1 Furthermore, they are essential to maintaining the standard of living for a significant portion of the global population.2 The following decades are predicted to see a sharp rise in the number of HVAC systems installed, mostly due to economic expansion, global warming and improved living standards.3,4 The effectiveness of HVAC systems can be judged by their ability to achieve thermal comfort and indoor air quality with minimal energy consumption. Based on such HVAC working efficiency requirements, indirect solutions such as passive architectural strategies were proposed to reduce the thermal load of HVAC systems so that their working time becomes lesser and thus reduced energy consumption. These architectural strategies include, for example, proper building
orientation, increasing building envelope insulation and using shading devices, namely external screens and louvres, as outlined in Palmero-Marrero and Oliveira.5 System engineering approaches can also contribute significantly to HVAC working efficiency requirements. In essence, the integrity of the system model; and compatibility of the control system are crucial for achieving the best results. The fundamental approach to achieving HVAC system model integrity is a proper understanding of the system structure, the internal interactions and the system's performance through incorporating the mathematical

In this sense, the need for comprehensive HVAC modelling and using systematic, scientific, multivariable feedback controller design methodology is a prerequisite. If not, energy savings and operational efficiency, which are important in constructing environmentally friendly buildings, would not be achieved.<sup>6</sup>
According to Whalley and Abdul-Ameer, comprehensive modelling can be obtained by considering the inlet and extraction fans as lumped parameter realizations which provide accurate, reliable modelling methods and keeps complexity to a minimum. This will allow the pressure changes at the inlet and outlet, to and from the ventilated space, to be adjusted by voltage variations across the fan motors. However, the dimensions of ventilated volume demand a distributed parameter modelling approach where the system's physical properties are distributed along the length of the system itself. With advanced automatic control application, these modelling methods permit the computation of the varying airflow dynamics.
Control System is an engineering design employed by process engineers to dictate some or all related process variables or states to provide process desired output responses in terms of dynamic and steadystate behaviours. The control system's design must also have the capability to deal with unexpected external interferences, changing loads and disturbances so it can restore the system's behaviour to the originally desired reference inputs.8 From the perspective of automatic control theory, the importance of the control system arises when there is often little prospect and difficulty obtaining a state vector to regulate an industrial process in practice. Furthermore, estimating the process states using observers or filters might implicate too much complexity and creates less assertion. Therefore, directly measuring the system output vector available for feedback purposes is a better way to regulate an industrial process. However, the employment of an incomplete output vector limits the choice of the controller design method and includes some restrictions.9 Examples can be experienced when employing the 'pole assignment' control strategy; so, as highlighted by Davison, 10 a part of the system poles in the open-loop configuration can be forced to a pre-confirmed location in the s-plane employing an individual proportional controller. In contrast, the rest of the poles migrate arbitrarily. But, such a situation creates a serious performance gap and constrains many application studies. Hence, locations of the whole set of the poles related to the open-loop system can be prescribed by using output measurements alone which had been recommended by Patel and Munro.<sup>11</sup> However, the approach necessitates the employment of dynamic controllers because such
dynamics can seriously affect the system performance before reaching the steady-state response. Furthermore, the problem reduces to the implementation matter as the controller-related computed dynamics cannot be tolerated due to high gains, noise amplification problems, non-minimum phase elements, etc., which are considered undesirable. Alternatively, the designer can identify poles and zeros that draw the closed poles to a desired location in the s-plane by using polynomial functions generated by the controller employed in conjunction with the naturally occurring system outputs. Practically, all the closed-loop system poles and zeros can be located using well-proven frequency-domain techniques. Consequently, single-loop and multivariable techniques combined, the Nyquist Array method as illustrated by Rosenbrock, 12 can be used, employing phase lag-lead networks, when requested to achieve an improved HVAC multivariable system performance.
Consequently, a comprehensive HVAC system model that accommodates all the possible components, dynamics and internal interactions of the system ending with a multivariable HVAC model along with a proper multivariable closed-loop feedback control strategy can achieve HVAC operational efficiency and thus optimized energy consumption.
#### **HVAC** mathematical model
Mathematical models are widely used for many aspects, such as operator training, simulation and fault diagnosis. <sup>13</sup> They can also be used for some industrial processes that cannot be constructed within laboratories to measure and analyse their behaviour. Nevertheless, a small test zone was used to describe its thermal and moisture behaviour as studied in Virk et al.14 Typically, HVAC systems are too large for laboratory studies because of the size of components; for instance, long air-ways and large ventilated volumes, 15 so a practical solution would be modelling the system mathematically. However, the accuracy of the model representation is vital to obtaining reliable predicted results. The outcome of reviewing HVAC modelling works reveals that most of the HVAC models were fragmented into one or more individual components. Hence, an HVAC model represents a single loop model or multiple independent loops, each with one controlled variable to avoid reaching a complete HVAC plant. This avoidance might be caused by the anticipated complexity resulting in a comprehensive HVAC mathematical model. However, few multivariable modelling approaches were also explored. In Preglei et al.. 16 the HVAC multivariable modelling was confined to a test plant consisting of a fan, heating and cooling coils, and a steam humidifier, but, the conditioned zone model still was not explicitly included in a final mathematical model. The researchers in Satyavada et al.<sup>17</sup> presented an integrated model
of an HVAC system with a boiler, radiator, AHU, thermal zone, valve, damper, fan, pump, pipes and ducts. A recirculating damper was also designed in the model to allow the amount of return air and fresh air to be mixed and to be changed in accordance with the damper control signal. Conversely, the final transfer function matrix converted from mathematical differential equations explaining the system dynamics behaviour with the analysis of the applied control technique was not presented.
Physics-based or white box HVAC modelling is also a technique where it employs mass and energy conservation, as well as heat transfer Equations taking into consideration the full knowledge of the concerned process.<sup>18</sup> Equations, as described by the laws of Darcy (law of water flow), Fick (law of gaseous flow) and Fourier (law of heat flow), were used by Lü<sup>19</sup> to derive a model that predicts indoor thermal conditions. Similarly, the authors in Tashtoush et al.<sup>20</sup> developed a dynamic model based on Equations of energy and mass balance incorporating HVAC system components, such as room zone, cooler, heater, fan, humidifier, dehumidifier and ducts. They were conscious of the dispersed properties of the system, but they did not take the extra mile to consider the dispersed nature of the physical process in the modelling procedure due to the complexity incorporated in the model derivation method.
Nevertheless, due to the complex structure of complete HVAC plants, which involve many parameters governing their performance, data-driven or black box modelling methodology is sometimes preferred as it is a straightforward procedure for deriving HVAC system models. Probability Density Functions (PDF) is an example of such an approach. It is a statistical prediction method that addresses the probability distribution of a continuous random variable of a process. Modelling by predicting the weather and the room occupancy by using the Probability Density Functions (PDF) technique to identify the building thermal load was followed by Ma et al., <sup>21</sup> Hong and Jiang, <sup>22</sup> and Zlatanović et al. <sup>23</sup>
Another modelling approach, namely the grey box modelling technique followed by Wu and Sun<sup>24</sup> and Li et al.<sup>25</sup> was proposed to use the physics-based Equations to build the process model while the values of the parameters can be identified by the measured data, which can be obtained by the manufacturer's operational data included in the catalogue or through a system commissioning procedure. It is worthy to mention that such models might be able to encompass the whole physical properties of the HVAC plant reaching a comprehensive model, but developing the transfer function matrix of the resulting multivariable model in the frequency domain was always missing, which is the basis of systematic, scientific, multivariable, feedback controller design methodologies.
On the one hand, HVAC for large ventilated volume is characterized by spatially and dimensional
dispersed system components such as long ventilated volume where the physical properties of air such as flow, temperature, and pressure are distributed along with the component. A similar model for airflow in a long road tunnel is recognized in Bartlett and Whalley. 26 Other components such as motors can be modelled as pointwise lumped parameters. On the other hand, considering the modelling of a building envelope, indoor space, and HVAC electrical and mechanical components creates a comprehensive HVAC multivariable model. It should be noted that such a model will lead to heavy couplings between the outputs which lead to a situation of an input change affecting all the system outputs. Despite the difficulties and the extensive mathematical operations used to decouple the interaction between the system outputs caused by a multivariable system, it can provide a model that can be, along with a compatible control strategy, the basis to secure improved HVAC system performance, thus energy-efficient building.
Based on the previous discussions, a hybrid distributed parameter-lumped model developed by Whalley and Abdul-Ameer is a good practical approach to represent a general HVAC system enabling compact modelling of large-scale HVAC systems. As the authors have considered the slenderness effect of some HVAC plant components, such as the long tunnel ventilated volume, where the ratio of length to diameter is high, an accurate model close to reality can be obtained. This model incorporates distributed parameter elements as well as concentrated lumped point-wise elements. It enables constructing the analytical model realizations that integrate all the dispersed salient dynamics of the system, including the finite time delay. In the meantime, without affecting the accuracy, lumped modelling is entirely appropriate for duct terminals, such as inlet, exit fan motors, and chilled water pump motors, due to their point-wise physical nature. More energy efficiency can be achieved by the installation of a recirculation duct reducing the thermal load on the cooling unit. However, time delays are incorporated in the final model, which makes it difficult to apply some control strategies.
Therefore, a readily derived model in the form of the time domain is found in Whalley and Abdul-Ameer<sup>7</sup> and approved to be used in this study. The final model also incorporated the mathematical Equations that govern the variations of air stream temperature with the mathematical hybrid lumped distributed parameter model. These temperature variations are caused by (i) airflow, and pressure changes at the inlet to the indoor ventilated space, (ii) changes in air temperature caused by circulation and air conditioning effects and (iii) temperature changes caused by changes in airflow at the exit from the indoor ventilated space. The model has also considered the typical losses related to the circulation network, ducting, dynamic impedance, and steady-state friction.
This study avoids reinventing the wheel to derive the complete mathematical model as it is already available in Whalley and Abdul-Ameer.7 Based on being comprehensive, it is quite practical enough to tackle and process the time domain graphical responses of this model, aiming to convert them into a transfer function matrix representing the frequency domain of the system. In addition to the multivariable decoupling control strategy used as illustrated in the upcoming sections, identification of the transfer function in Laplace Transform are the two significances of the study
## Multivariable control techniques
Today's advanced HVAC systems are designed with multiple inputs interacting on different levels with multiple outputs. Meanwhile, according to MacFarlane,27 multivariable system control application is specified with some restrictions like the internal interactions between the various system outputs, which influence each other. A conceptual two-step approach can be followed to control a multivariable system. The first is to decouple the interactions in the system transfer function so that any alteration in a system input can affect only the corresponding output. The second step is to design a proper single input single output control technique similar to those used in SISO processes.28
Certain techniques were used to decouple the multivariable system, such as the one used in O¨zgo¨ren,29 which presumes that virtual control inputs would have a decoupled, non-interactive effect on the outputs of interest. Decoupling a multivariable model by including a steady-state matrix with a low coupling percentage in the feedback control law has been approached by Whalley and Ebrahimi.30 However, the familiar approach to decouple internal loops in a multivariable system is to design a matrix of compensators to decouple the multivariable system into multiple individual loops. Many techniques to achieve such essential steps were proposed, such as the pseudo-diagonalization procedure employed in Hawkins.31
A British school-related control technique, namely Nyquist-Array in either inverse or direct array, is a multivariable control technique that combines the competency of modern algebra with the analytical procedures of classical control theory. It examines whether the internal coupling of the multivariable model is reduced or not. In addition to the Nyquist Array technique, the characteristic loci technique has also been following the same decoupling approach and reviewed in MacFarlane and Kouvaritakis.32 The H' loop-shaping design procedure also has a decoupling technique by initially developing a precompensator matrix to create a plant with desirable properties. The primary distinction in this approach
is that the matrix of the pre-compensators used in the decoupling procedure is a totally multivariable controller designed using optimization.
Several ways were researched to achieve dominance with the employment of a matrix of compensators. Obtaining a dominant matrix allows for the creation of simple controllers when other approaches would call for more complicated ones. But reaching a dominant diagonal matrix usually depends on trial and error. Therefore, more advancement in this direction is still required. The Nyquist-Array multivariable control strategy is an effective tool for multivariable control system design and analysis. Using this approach, the multivariable problem is typically divided into nearly non-interactive single-input/single-output feedback problems, which can then be resolved using conventional control design techniques. Although finding the matrix of compensators is not a trivial task, the Nyquist Direct Array control technique will be employed in this study due to its capability to reduce the internal interactions of the system, and then normal achievable classic SISO feedback controllers can be applied, aiming to obtain well-behaved HVAC system performance
# Extracting HVAC transfer function matrix
In the selected model developed by Whalley and Abdul-Ameer,7 the authors used MATLAB and SIMULATION software to simulate the system output graphical responses in the open-loop system configuration. Extracting the frequency domain of the model can be done by undertaking these open-loop system time-domain graphical responses and converting them into the frequency domain responses in Laplace 's' variable representation, creating a threeinput thee-outputs multivariable model. The multivariable input-output relationship is getting the following form:

#### System identification
This is the most important research stage, which is developing a transfer function matrix of the selected model. The developed transfer function model will be afterwards the basis for applying a suitable control strategy. MATLAB Toolbox of System Identification is used to extract the transfer function elements in Laplace variable representations. The procedure incorporates three steps. In the first, the graphical dynamical response illustrating a model open loop output, as shown in Whalley and Abdul-Ameer, will be processed to identify the (x, y) coordinates of the response curve itself. This response is supposed to embody salient dynamic characteristics of the system behaviour. Second, the identified (x, y) coordinates are introduced to MATLAB System Identification
generated with defined parameters which are mainly the coefficients of the numerator and denominator polynomials. It also gives the percentage of data fit, which means how much-fit the ratio of the transfer function is against the time domain data fed to the system. The coordinates of the open loop graphical model response are indeed a group of abscissa and ordinate pairs. The abscissa of a point is how far from the origin the point is on the horizontal or x - axis, while the ordinate of a point is the value that tells how far from the origin the point is on the vertical or v - axis. #### Process of transfer function reduction
Transfer function order reduction is required because multivariable control techniques incorporate complicated mathematical and algebraic operations. The reduction must consider keeping the original model's major dynamics and characteristics, which are crucial for the industrial process application performance. There are many methods that can be used to reduce the model order; the one used in this study is the Pole-Zero simplification which eliminates the similar or near pole-zero pairs. As an outcome of applying the Pole-Zero simplification procedure by MATLAB Model Reduction Application, the reduced G_{red}(s) elements are shown in matrix equation (3). Figures 1 to 3 illustrate also the responses of transfer function elements of G_{red}(s) superimposed with the responses
of original higher-order transfer functions G(s) elements. The responses show a satisfactory relative overlapping of originally derived transfer functions in comparison to the reduced-order transfer functions maintaining almost the same transient and steady-state characteristics. This difference must be slight and minor as showed in the figures maintaining the original dynamics of the steady state and time constant otherwise order reduction wouldn't be useful.
$$ G_{red}(s) = \begin{bmatrix} \frac{0.001319}{s + 0.03509} & \frac{-0.02386}{3.5s + 0.2137} & \frac{0.002003}{2.8s + 0.05175} \\ \frac{-0.007193 + 0.004349}{s^2 + 0.08724s + 0.001237} & \frac{-0.06996}{s + 0.006335} & \frac{0.02223}{s + 0.006335} \\ \frac{-0.003539}{1.4s + 0.04581} & \frac{-0.005388}{7s + 0.4465} & \frac{0.0001918}{2.228s + 0.04609} \end{bmatrix} (3) $$
#### **Control objectives **
Referring to the open-loop system responses in Figures 1 to 3, it can be observed that significant coupling exists between the output responses so that any step change at any of the system inputs causes corresponding variations in all system outputs. The error at the steady state is obvious, but the system is stable, showing no oscillation around the steady-state value. As a result, reducing the coupling between the outputs should be one of the control objectives. Meanwhile,
the system in the closed feedback control must show stability and behave satisfactorily in terms of steadystate error and settling time.
Furthermore, HVAC systems are exposed to many sources of disturbances. Hence, the closed feedback control has to be able to reject such disturbances with the least time and energy dissipation.
# **Direct Nyquist Array (DNA) **
Direct Nyquist Array (DNA) is a multivariable control technique where the feedback control problem related to multivariable system is reduced to a set of single closed-loop control designs. The procedure is based on reducing the interactions between system outputs by decoupling them so that a closed-loop control technique can be applied to each decoupled loop independently.
#### System decoupling
The decoupling procedure incorporates designing a matrix of compensators K(s) so that when it is multiplied by the plant transfer function G_{red}(s), the product is a diagonally dominant matrix. Afterwards, a closed-loop control technique can be applied to each loop independently. Mathematically, diagonal dominant means that the amplitude of any diagonal-location matrix element is greater than the summation of the amplitudes of the off-diagonal matrix elements for a row or a column. If m \times m, A(s) is a complex elements matrix, then:
A(s) can be said diagonal row dominant when:
$$ |a_{ii}(s)| > \sum_{\substack{j=1\\i\neq j}}^{m} |a_{ij}(s)| \tag{4} $$
for all i = 1, 2, \dots, m and a_{ii}(s) is a diagonal element.
However, A(s) can be said column dominant when:
$$ |a_{ii}(s)| > \sum_{\substack{j=1\\i\neq j}}^{m} |a_{ji}(s)| \tag{5} $$
for all i = 1, 2, \dots, m.
A mixture of row and column dominance is not applicable for a matrix to be diagonal dominance, so either definition will be enough.<sup>33</sup> The diagonal dominant matrix can be also investigated graphically. A row in a matrix is graphically dominant when the union of circles centred by a_{ii}(s) with a radius value calculated by equation (6) at an extended certain range of frequencies exclude the origin of the complex plane.
$$ r_i = \sum_{\substack{j=1\\i\neq j}}^m \left| a_{ij}(s) \right| \tag{6} $$
The trial and error approach to identify the decoupling pre-compensators with no guarantee to yield a solution is the familiar approach.<sup>23</sup> The complexity of the exercise increases with a multivariable system of a three-input three-output size. Alternatively, using a systematic way of solving a system of equations that can result from the multiplication of matrices as in equation (7) will be followed to calculate the precompensators elements with the aid of MATLAB.
A(s) elements can be selected purposely fulfilling equations (4) and (6). Accordingly, the matrix equation (8) is developed so that with an insight into this matrix, it can be realized that the value of the matrix diagonal element at any frequency is clearly higher than the sum of row off-diagonal elements at the same frequency
Since A(s) and G_{red}(s) are known matrices up to this stage, therefore, K(s) elements can be calculated mathematically with the aid of MATLAB software employing equation (7).
$$ A(s) = G_{red}(s)K(s) \tag{7} $$

These compensators can be reduced to a multiplication of gain, first and secondorder lead-lag compensators. Some compensators include zeros and unstable poles whose locations are on the left side of the s-plane and some of them are located on the imaginary axis. Practically compensators with unstable poles should be avoided because their role is to stabilize the system. However, the approach herein is totally different as the designed compensators merely serve as 'decoupling commentators' so that the entire decoupled system G_{red}(s)K(s) can be stabilized using PID controllers.
## Gershgorin circles
Next is to visualize the decoupling effect by plotting the Nyquist contour of each diagonal element a_{ii}(s) of A(s) matrix which is a connection of points representing the centres of the Gershgorin circles at each point of frequency in the complex plane. The range of frequencies considered in this study varies from (0.1) to (10^6) rad/sec which represent frequencies that industrial processes work within. The Gershgorin band is
then established by the circles centred around a_{ii}(j\omega) points and with radii of:
$$ \sum_{\substack{j=1\\j\neq i}}^{3} a_{ji}(j\omega) \text{ for a row at the range from } (0.1) \text{ to} $$
(10<sup>6</sup>)rad/sec frequencies.
If the Gershgorin bands are not encircling the complex plane origin, then A(s) matrix is said to be a diagonally dominant matrix. More diagonal dominance corresponds with a narrower Gershgorin band thus more cross-decoupling between the system outputs. Meanwhile, the wider Gershgorin band corresponds to less diagonal dominance and then reflected on less cross-decoupling effect between the system outputs.

#### System stability test
The stability of the system at closed-loop configuration can be examined by forming Gershgorin bands for the open-loop matrix equation in (10). Criterion of Nyquist stability for multivariable systems is explained as follows:
If the Gershgorin bands, encircle the complex point of (-1,0J) by a number of times equal to (N_i), the system under the closed-loop loop configuration is stable if and only if:
$$ \sum_{i=1}^{m} N_i = p_0 \tag{11} $$
(p_0) is number of H(s) poles which is an open-loop configuration positioned at the right of the s-plane imaginary axis. Usually, most open-loop industrial processes are stable so that (p_0 = 0), similar assumption is considered in this paper. Stability Gershgorin bands are centred about the diagonal elements h_{ii}(s) of open-loop transfer function H(s), where 1, 2, \dots, m with radii equal to summation of all elements of a particular row or column except the diagonal element h_{ii}(s).

# Conclusion
An HVAC system is classified as a building's highest energy consumer. Reliable and accurate HVAC mathematical models, as well as a suitable control strategy, are part of the efforts to achieve greater
building energy efficiency. This study followed a thorough exploration method to identify an accurate, comprehensive, mathematically HVAC system model, mainly a hybrid distributed parameterlumped model. It enables constructing the analytical model realizations that integrate all the dispersed salient dynamics of the long-ventilated volume, including the finite time delay. In the meantime, without affecting the accuracy, lumped modelling is entirely appropriate for duct terminals, such as inlet and exit fan motors, as well as chilled water pump motors. Since the transfer function matrix was not developed in the approved model-related article, it was exclusively developed in this study employing System Identification Application by MATLAB and using the graphical time domain responses. The transfer function matrix becomes the basis for systematic, scientific, multivariable feedback controller design. Following two conventional steps, Direct Nyquist Array (DNA) control strategy is applied to the derived transfer function matrix. In the first step, it successfully managed to decouple the HVAC system into three separate single input single output (SISO) loops and afterwards, a feedback control technique, mainly PID, is used for each loop individually in the second step. According to the results obtained, the system's outputs are decoupled with a very low coupling percentage, which means that each change in a system input only affects the associated system output. The underdamped system output responses and practically negligible steady-state error demonstrate the effectiveness of the chosen PID parameters.
In contrast to the open-loop response time of (200–600) s, the values of steady-state responses in the closed-loop configuration are obtained in (10–15) s speeding up the responses. However, different overshoot percentages in the responses are observed, but they are often negligible and settle quickly. Thus, they have little impact on the ventilated volume's thermal comfort. The Nyquist criterion for system stability has also been investigated and confirmed to satisfy the requirement. The SISO closed-loop PID controllers and the multivariable DNA control technology have demonstrated the ability to suppress outside disturbances and return the system to its original functional steady-state values.
